core: Economic effects of taxation, public budgets and redistribution
Economic decisions, business/finance and legal institutions
adjacent: Business taxation, reporting and international fiscal structures
questions: How do tax and spending choices affect households, firms and welfare?
How can evidence and ethical reasoning evaluate tax-policy choices?

trace: Actual legal foundations, institutions, justice and public/private law supply legal context for economic regulation, without teaching fiscal legislation.
Actual firm organisation, stakeholders, business decisions and value creation provide business context for economic effects on firms; no tax-planning sequence.
Actual micro/macro models, incentives, strategic interaction and market/aggregate analysis provide substantive foundations for fiscal-policy questions.
Actual measurement, survey/experimental design, sampling, inference and introductory regression supply empirical tools; not a fiscal-methods specialisation.
Actual international legal sources, responsibility and institutions provide a bounded legal framework; no tax treaties or international tax doctrine are inferred.
Actual constitutional/public institutions and administrative principles support government/regulation inquiry; not Dutch fiscal procedure.
International-relations theories, institutions and country-position research provide specific context for cross-border political/economic decisions, not international tax law.
Actual rights, dignity, equality and legal/philosophical argument add normative criteria for fairness questions; no specialised taxpayer-rights doctrine.
Description-only: actual psychological deviations, biases, framing and experiments extend economic decision analysis; tax-compliance experiments are not promised.
Actual macroeconomic models, growth, expectations, fiscal/monetary policy and open economies provide substantive fiscal-policy/economic-effects analysis.

Actual financial statements, management accounting, budgets, costs and discounted investment appraisal supply accounting/firm substance. One course does not reproduce three financial-reporting stages, advanced tax accounting or taxable-profit computation.
Actual EU institutions, competences, free movement and enforcement supply EU legal foundations, not state-aid/direct-tax analysis as a specialised fiscal sequence.

Actual labour/capital markets, market power, externalities and government intervention give economic tools for analysing fiscal incidence/incentives. Detailed tax-law applications are not asserted as taught.

Actual public goods, efficiency/equity, expenditure, health/welfare/social insurance, taxation and redistribution directly sustain public-finance inquiry. This goes beyond generic economic coherence, but does not reproduce Dutch tax-base/rate doctrine.
Description-only: policy-making phases, alternative conceptualisations and policy memos through a sugar case support policy analysis; the case is not automatically a taught tax experiment.

Actual property/tort/contract doctrine and comparative IRAC/case research, including France/Germany/England/China/US, provide substantive private-law context for business decisions. No fiscal statute or Dutch tax computation is inferred.
Actual European decision rules, actors and policy-document inquiry supply political/institutional context for cross-border fiscal-policy questions.
Actual international business strategy, institutional governance and ethics support analysis of multinational business decisions; not international tax structures/treaty planning.
Actual data cleaning, transformation, visualisation and exploratory questions supply concrete empirical workflow; a tax dataset or project is not guaranteed.
Description-only: OLS/GLS/instrumental variables, inference, Monte Carlo work and an empirical paper sustain economic causal/predictive inquiry. No fiscal dissertation equivalence.
Actual asset valuation, risk, banking regulation and financial instruments supply finance and investment context; not complete advanced corporate finance or tax accounting.
Actual qualitative design, interviews, coding/reflexivity and a team inquiry supply qualitative empirical methods; no fiscal interview project is guaranteed.
Actual consequentialist/Kantian/virtue/feminist theories and close argumentative reading supply substantive ethical judgement for fairness questions without being a specialised fiscal-ethics course.

alternatives.label: Economics, public finance and policy
alternatives.concept: A programme examining how economic incentives, public spending and taxation affect households, firms and social welfare. Microeconomics, macroeconomics, behavioural economics and public economics combine with accounting, finance, legal institutions and empirical methods. Policy analysis and ethics evaluate collective choices. This is broader economic-policy study, without the statutory fiscal, advanced-reporting or tax-research specialisation of Fiscal Economics.
alternatives.labelReason: All six current economics courses plus substantive accounting, finance and empirical research sustain the economic/public-finance label; the programme is not called Fiscal Economics or Tax Law.
progression: All covered offerings and earlier formal prerequisites checked. PPD is in year one; BENGATE102 precedes advanced economics and legal foundation precedes legal dependents.

candidates.label: Business taxation and advanced financial reporting
candidates.reason: Actual Accounting/Corporate Finance, banking, private/business law and international business are genuine contributions and were tested with a full business-context schedule. Organisational/communication substitutions do not supply further statutory business taxation, advanced reporting or tax-base computation to anchor a distinct fiscal-business programme.

candidates.label: International fiscal structures
candidates.reason: Actual international macroeconomics, EU/public international law and international business supply cross-border institutional/economic analysis. They do not teach tax-treaty allocation, transfer pricing or fiscal structuring as sustained specialist study. No distinct full international-tax programme is established.

selection.assessment: One strongest broad economic/public-finance response accepted. All six actual economics courses, including behavioural work, are now in the closest option; the prior policy/behaviour test no longer establishes a stronger distinct direction. Business and international fiscal specialisations lack further taught fiscal/accounting substance. No default second or third option.

blocks: Both establish foundational microeconomic analysis; UCR also introduces macroeconomics rather than supplying the identical dedicated course.
Both study macroeconomic outcomes and policy. UCR uses open-economy and later macroeconomic models; institutional and level emphases differ.

Both directly study public-finance theory, government revenues/expenditure and redistribution. UvA specifically includes Dutch tax and spending arrangements; UCR provides broader public-economics models and applications.
Both directly teach foundational accounting/financial statements. UCR also introduces managerial accounting and investment appraisal; one course is not the advanced reporting sequence.
Both teach substantive property/private-law reasoning. UCR compares several systems and also tort/contract; the precise Dutch-law course is not reproduced.
Both address valuation, financial risk and instruments. UCR has banking/asset-pricing emphasis and does not replace all later finance.
Both develop quantitative analysis, descriptive/inferential reasoning and measurement. UCR includes research design; no claim that the external course explicitly teaches regression.
Both include qualitative empirical inquiry. UCR supplies interviews/coding/reflexivity and team research with different subject-specific assignments.

notes.text: UCR offers broader economics and public-finance inquiry. It does not provide the cumulative statutory-tax sequence, advanced financial reporting, corporate/VAT/payroll and international tax training, taxable-profit calculation or required fiscal seminar and thesis.

audience.programmeDescription: Fiscal Economics studies taxation and its economic effects on governments, firms and households, combining economic analysis with tax law, accounting, finance and ethical judgement. Later study develops specialised fiscal and reporting knowledge and culminates in a seminar and thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: A broader UCR programme in economics, public finance and policy meaningfully responds to the confirmed economic-effects and fiscal-policy inquiry, while supplying substantially less statutory-tax and advanced-accounting specialisation. UCR directly studies taxation and redistribution through public economics and supports economic-effects inquiry through microeconomics, macroeconomics, behavioural analysis and empirical methods. Its general legal and accounting courses do not reproduce specialist fiscal-law analysis or advanced reporting.

componentNotes.y1-orientation-econ-law: Introduces economic analysis of law and the legal constraints on economic policy, including tax law.
componentNotes.y1-foundations-1: Introduces economic and business concepts such as incentives, firms, markets, public goods and regulation, with critical reading of academic literature.
componentNotes.y1-foundations-2: Combines study and academic skills with economic, fiscal, ethical and sustainability questions about digital platforms.
componentNotes.y1-financial-accounting-1: Introduces transaction recording, accrual accounting, assets, liabilities and financial statements.
componentNotes.y1-microeconomics-1: Studies consumer and producer choices, markets, efficiency, market failure and strategic interaction.
componentNotes.y1-macroeconomics-1: Studies aggregate economic activity, banks, money, growth and business cycles using macroeconomic models.
componentNotes.y1-quantitative-analysis-1: Develops probability, statistical inference, confidence intervals and analysis of relationships using SPSS.
componentNotes.y1-finance-1: Introduces time value of money, investment appraisal, valuation, risk and return, and working-capital management.
componentNotes.y1-orientation-fiscal-econ: Introduces income, payroll, corporate, consumption, inheritance and gift taxes and their relationships.
componentNotes.y1-qualitative-project: A small-group qualitative research project investigates a problem in real organisations. Associated skills work develops Excel and presentation skills.
componentNotes.y2-general-tax: Introduces income taxation and payroll levies as preparation for advanced fiscal study.
componentNotes.y2-property-law: Studies Dutch private law, obligations, employment contracts, liability and rights over property.
componentNotes.y2-business-tax: Introduces fiscal profit determination, corporate income taxation and VAT, preparing later specialist tax courses.
componentNotes.y2-company-reporting-law: Studies partnerships and companies, governance, liability, restructuring and annual-reporting law, including commercial and fiscal accounts.
componentNotes.y2-tax-government: Examines public finance, taxation, social spending, public debt, redistribution and intergenerational questions.
componentNotes.y2-financial-accounting-2: Develops financial reporting for assets, liabilities, equity, revenue and cash flows. The programme accepts its first-year Financial Accounting 1 for Economics as preparation.
componentNotes.y2-management-accounting-1: Studies cost and performance information used for pricing, investment, planning and organisational decisions.
componentNotes.y2-financial-accounting-3: Develops advanced financial reporting, including consolidation, pensions, income taxes, leases and disclosure. Financial Accounting 2 provides recommended preparation.
componentNotes.y2-fiscal-methodology: Examines taxation as a moral phenomenon, tax principles, philosophy of science, international tax competition and professional ethics.
componentNotes.y2-tax-technology: A 3 EC course examines interactions between technology and taxation, including crypto-assets, information exchange, AI and tax policy.
componentNotes.y2-payroll-tax: A 3 EC course applies wage-tax and social-insurance rules to practical cases and employment conditions.
componentNotes.y3-bound-elective: This example selects a 6 EC option on corporate responsibility, stakeholders and sustainability. The course is open to Economics and Business bachelor students.
componentNotes.y3-tax-procedure: Studies formal obligations through the tax-return and assessment cycle, including taxpayer rights, legal protection, interest and administrative penalties.
componentNotes.y3-corporate-tax: Studies corporate taxation, including contributions and distributions, interest limitations, participation exemptions, fiscal unity and loss relief.
componentNotes.y3-vat: Develops specialist understanding of taxable transactions and deduction of input VAT.
componentNotes.y3-international-tax: Studies taxing rights, double-taxation relief, cross-border liabilities, withholding taxes and tax treaties.
componentNotes.y3-dga-tax: Studies the fiscal position of directors and major shareholders, including substantial-shareholdings, succession, payroll and transfers into a company.
componentNotes.y3-finance-2: Builds on Finance 1 to study financing and investment, valuation, capital structure, options, payout policy and governance.
componentNotes.y3-graduation-seminar: A 6 EC seminar develops the thesis question, research approach, introduction and first literature chapter. Entry requires completion of years one and two and at least 120 EC. Specialist tax courses are recommended preparation.
componentNotes.y3-profit-calculation: Studies fiscal total and annual profit and their relationship to profit measures used in financial reporting.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: A 6 EC individual thesis follows the Fiscal Economics Graduation Seminar. Students deepen their research and analysis and submit progress reports; a final discussion may be required by the coordinator.
